lessons.title: Study Session 1: Choosing a Store Platform That Fits the Business

blocks.text: Introduction Blessings Kaunda sells handmade soap and skincare products from Kasungu, and had chosen his store platform because it was the one his cousin used for a catalog several times the size of his own, only realising months later that he was paying monthly fees for inventory tools he never touched while bumping against a hard limit on how many products he could list. 1.0 Learning Outcomes By the end of this study session, you should be able to: Explain what research found about the factors small and medium enterprises weigh when choosing an e-commerce platform. Distinguish a platform chosen by comparison to another business from one chosen by fit. Apply a method for matching a platform's plan, fees and limits to a business's actual size and growth plans. Recognise the warning signs that a store has outgrown, or never fit, its current platform. 2.0 Main Content 2.1 A Platform Chosen by Comparison, Not by Fit Blessings Kaunda's soap and skincare business in Kasungu ran on a store platform he picked because his cousin used it successfully for a much larger general retail catalog. Blessings paid monthly for inventory management tools built for hundreds of products while listing barely a dozen, and only discovered a hard ceiling on product listings when he tried adding new seasonal scents ahead of a holiday rush and the platform simply would not let him. 2.2 What Research Found About Platform Selection Factors Wei-Hsi Chen, Yi-Ching Lin, Avishek Bag and Ching-Lin Chen studied the factors influencing small and medium-sized enterprises' and micro-enterprises' choice of cross-border e-commerce platform for a 2023 study based on interviews with Taiwanese companies. Economic, technological and social factors, including how well a platform's cost structure, scalability and ease of integration matched a business's actual size and stage, were found to shape platform choice far more reliably than which platform a comparable business happened to already be using. 2.3 Choosing a Platform Deliberately Matching Plan and Fees to Actual Catalog Size Comparing a platform's pricing tiers, transaction fees and product limits directly against a business's real, current catalog size, rather than the catalog of whichever business recommended it, avoids paying for capacity that goes unused or hitting a ceiling too early. Checking Room to Grow Before Committing Looking specifically at how a platform's plan changes as a business adds products, orders or staff accounts, before committing to it, reduces the chance of a second costly migration once the business outgrows what looked sufficient at the start. 2.4 Key Practices Compare a platform's fees and product limits against the business's actual current catalog size. Check how a platform's plan and pricing change as a business adds products or orders. Check a platform's fit against the business's own numbers, not against another business's success with it. Revisit the platform choice periodically as the business's own needs change. 2.5 A Worked Example: Blessings's Platform Comparison Blessings listed his actual product count, monthly order volume and the specific features he genuinely used, then compared three platforms against that list rather than against his cousin's catalog, finding a plan built for a ten-to-fifty-product store priced at roughly a third of what he had been paying. Blessings's original platform choice had made sense on paper, since his cousin's recommendation came from real, satisfied experience running a much larger store. The mismatch was never about the platform itself, but about comparing it to someone else's business instead of his own, and only measuring his own catalog against its plans and limits directly ever surfaced that difference. 2.6 Common Pitfalls Choosing a platform because a larger or differently structured business already uses it successfully overlooks whether its plan, fees and limits actually fit a much smaller catalog, precisely the trap Blessings fell into for months. Ignoring how a platform's plan and pricing change as a business grows can force a costly migration later, once limits that once seemed generous start to bind. 2.7 The Right Platform Fits the Business It Serves Blessings's soap and skincare products had always been strong sellers, and the platform switch changed nothing about their quality. What had held the business back was a platform sized for someone else's catalog rather than his own, and only comparing plans against his actual numbers ever revealed that a far better fit was available at a fraction of the cost. 3.0 Study Session Summary and Conclusion In this study session, you learned to choose a store platform that fits a business's actual size, fees and growth plans. Study Session 2 turns from choosing the platform itself to structuring the store built on it so customers can actually find what they came for.

Reflect and Grow — Self-Assessment 1. Think about your own store platform. Was it chosen by comparing it against your own catalog and growth plans, or against someone else's business? 2. Compare your current or planned platform's fees and limits directly against your real product count and order volume. Practical Output: Practical Output A platform comparison for one real business, matching fees, limits and features against its actual current catalog size and growth plans. 7.0 References and Further Reading Chen, W-H., Lin, Y-C., Bag, A., & Chen, C-L. (2023). Influence factors of small and medium-sized enterprises and micro-enterprises in the cross-border e-commerce platforms. Journal of Theoretical and Applied Electronic Commerce Research, 18(1), 416 to 440. Optional further reading, curriculum-team reviewed: Proverbs 14:8, on the wisdom of the prudent being to understand his own way, while the folly of fools is deceit. Qur'an, Surah Az-Zumar 39:39, on working according to one's own position and finding out in time what that yields.

lessons.title: Study Session 2: Structuring the Store So Customers Can Find What They Need

blocks.text: Introduction Providence Uwamahoro raises her two children alone in Nyanza while running a small online shop selling handwoven baskets, and had built her store's menu by adding a new category every time she listed a new basket style, until the storefront held nineteen categories for barely forty products and a customer looking for a simple laundry basket had to open six different menus before finding one. 1.0 Learning Outcomes By the end of this study session, you should be able to: Explain what research found about how a store's navigation design shapes a shopper's response to it. Distinguish a navigation structure built by accumulation from one built by design. Apply a method for structuring categories and navigation so a customer can find a product quickly. 2.0 Main Content 2.1 Nineteen Categories for Forty Products Providence Uwamahoro's basket shop grew its category list one entry at a time, a new menu item for nearly every new basket style, shape or occasion she listed. By the time she counted them, the store held nineteen categories for barely forty products, some named after a basket's shape, others after its material, and others after an occasion, so a customer looking for something as ordinary as a laundry basket had to open six separate menus before finding one. 2.2 What Research Found About Navigation and Customer Response Ruijuan Wu, Yan Li and Yixiao Hu examined how an apparel e-retailer's primary navigation shaped consumers' response for a 2022 study combining an eye-tracking experiment with two laboratory experiments. A store's navigation design was found to measurably shape a shopper's attention and willingness to engage further with the store, evidence that how a storefront is organised is not a neutral or invisible design choice. 2.3 Structuring Categories and Navigation by Design Grouping Products by How a Customer Actually Searches Organising categories around the way a customer is likely to search, by product type or use rather than by whichever attribute happened to come to mind when a product was listed, keeps related products together instead of scattered across near-duplicate categories. Keeping the Category List Short Enough to Scan Limiting the number of top-level categories to what a customer can scan in a glance, and moving finer distinctions into subcategories or filters, prevents a menu from growing one entry at a time into something no longer usable. 2.4 Key Practices Group products by how a customer is likely to search, not by whichever detail was top of mind when listing them. Keep the top-level category list short enough to scan at a glance. Move finer distinctions, such as shape or material, into subcategories or filters. 2.5 A Worked Example: Providence's Rebuilt Menu Providence listed all forty products alongside the actual words she had heard customers use to describe what they wanted, laundry basket, storage basket, gift basket, then rebuilt her menu around six of those real search terms, folding basket shape and material into filters inside each category rather than separate top-level menus. The nineteen-category menu had grown honestly, one addition at a time, out of real effort to describe each new basket accurately as it arrived. What it had never done was reflect how a customer actually searched for a basket, and only rebuilding the categories around real customer language ever closed that gap. 2.6 Common Pitfalls Adding a new category every time a new product arrives, without ever stepping back to reorganise, produces a menu that grows unusable long before anyone intended it to, the exact pattern behind Providence's nineteen categories. Naming categories after whichever attribute felt most natural at the moment of listing, rather than consistently, scatters related products across menus a customer would never think to check separately. 2.7 A Menu Reflects How It Grew, Not How Customers Search Providence's baskets had always been well made and fairly priced, and no customer complaint had ever questioned that. The barrier was a menu that reflected the order products had been added rather than the way a customer went looking for them, and only rebuilding it around real search language ever let customers reach a product the way they actually looked for it. 3.0 Study Session Summary and Conclusion In this study session, you learned to structure a store's categories and navigation around how a customer actually searches. Study Session 3 turns from the store's internal structure to the technical setup of payment and checkout that sits behind it.

Reflect and Grow — Self-Assessment 1. Think about your own store's categories. Do they reflect how a customer searches, or the order products were added? 2. Rebuild the category list for one real store around the actual words customers use to describe what they want. Practical Output: Practical Output A rebuilt category structure for one real store, organised around real customer search language rather than listing order. 7.0 References and Further Reading Wu, R., Li, Y., & Hu, Y. (2022). Navigating in online stores: The effect of the primary navigation on consumers' response, a study based on the apparel e-retailer. Electronic Commerce Research and Applications, 53, Article 101150. Optional further reading, curriculum-team reviewed: 1 Timothy 3:4, on managing one's own household well, with children kept respectful in every way. Qur'an, Surah An-Naml 27:75, on there being nothing hidden, in the heaven or the earth, but is in a clear record.
Evidence to keep Keep a written note, worksheet, reflection or practical output from this study session. Your progress should show real learning before the quiz.

lessons.title: Study Session 3: Setting Up Secure Payment and Checkout Infrastructure

blocks.text: Introduction Amélia Machava sells capulana fabric and ready-made clothing from Pemba through her own online store, and had connected a payment option a fellow seller recommended without checking whether a security certificate actually protected the connection, until a customer messaged asking why her browser was showing a warning that the site was not secure. 1.0 Learning Outcomes By the end of this study session, you should be able to: Explain what research found about trust, security and purchase decisions in e-commerce. Distinguish a checkout secured by a verified certificate from one that only appears secure. Apply a method for setting up and verifying a store's payment and checkout security. Recognise the warning signs a customer, or a browser, gives when a checkout is not properly secured. 2.0 Main Content 2.1 A Warning a Customer Saw Before Amélia Did Amélia Machava's fabric and clothing store in Pemba used a payment link a fellow seller had recommended, connected without any separate check of whether the page itself carried a valid security certificate. A regular customer, midway through a purchase, messaged to ask why her browser was flatly warning her the site was not secure, a warning Amélia had never seen for herself since she almost always checked out through her own already-trusted device. 2.2 What Research Found About Trust, Security and Purchase Decisions Sok Handoyo conducted a meta-analysis examining trust, perceived risk, perceived security and electronic word of mouth in e-commerce purchasing decisions, published in 2024. Perceived security was found to significantly influence a buyer's purchase decision, with perceived risk moderating how strongly trust translated into an actual completed purchase, meaning a checkout that looks or feels insecure can undo trust built everywhere else in the buying journey. 2.3 Setting Up and Verifying Checkout Security Installing and Verifying an SSL Certificate Installing a valid SSL certificate on the store's checkout pages, and confirming it directly in a browser rather than assuming a payment provider handled it automatically, closes the specific gap that produced Amélia's security warning. Connecting a Payment Gateway Built for the Business's Region and Currency Choosing a payment gateway that is actually built to process the currency, cards and mobile money options a business's real customers use, rather than whichever gateway a fellow seller happened to recommend, avoids failed or unsupported transactions at checkout. 2.4 Key Practices Install a valid SSL certificate on every checkout page and verify it directly in a browser. Choose a payment gateway built for the business's actual region, currency and payment methods. Check the checkout for a browser security warning after any change to the store. Confirm a payment provider's security claims rather than assuming them. 2.5 A Worked Example: Amélia's Verified Checkout Amélia contacted her hosting provider to install a proper SSL certificate rather than relying on the payment link alone, then checked the browser bar herself on a phone and a computer to confirm the warning was gone, also switching to a payment gateway that supported the mobile money option most of her customers actually used. Amélia's original setup had worked well enough that payments were still going through, so nothing about it seemed obviously broken from her side of the screen. The certificate a customer's browser checks for had never been part of the setup at all, and only installing and personally verifying one ever removed the warning a customer, not Amélia, had been the one to notice first. 2.6 Common Pitfalls Adopting a payment link or method because another seller recommended it, without separately confirming the checkout is actually secured by a valid certificate, can leave a warning visible to every customer long before the seller ever notices anything wrong. Assuming a payment provider automatically handles every layer of checkout security removes the one check that would have caught Amélia's missing certificate sooner. 2.7 Security a Customer Can See Is Security That Gets Used Amélia's fabric and clothing had never been the problem, and her prices had stayed competitive throughout. The gap sat specifically in a checkout that looked, to a customer's browser, less secure than it needed to, and only installing and verifying a proper certificate ever closed that visible gap between a genuine purchase intention and a completed sale. 3.0 Study Session Summary and Conclusion In this study session, you learned to set up and verify secure payment and checkout infrastructure. Study Session 4 turns from securing the checkout moment itself to protecting the store and its customer data more broadly.

Reflect and Grow — Self-Assessment 1. Think about your own checkout. Have you personally verified its security certificate, or only assumed a provider handled it? 2. Check your own store's checkout for a browser security warning, and confirm whether a valid certificate is actually installed. Practical Output: Practical Output A verified payment and checkout security check for one real online store, confirming a valid certificate and a suitable payment gateway. 7.0 References and Further Reading Handoyo, S. (2024). Purchasing in the digital age: A meta-analytical perspective on trust, risk, security, and e-WOM in e-commerce. Heliyon, 10(8), Article e29714. Optional further reading, curriculum-team reviewed: Ezekiel 33:6, on the watchman who sees danger coming and must sound the warning, or bear responsibility for what follows. Qur'an, Surah Al-Ma'arij 70:32, on those who are attentive to their trusts and their promises.
Evidence to keep Keep a written note, worksheet, reflection or practical output from this study session. Your progress should show real learning before the quiz.

lessons.title: Study Session 4: Protecting the Store and Customer Data

blocks.text: Introduction Brice Fotso built a growing online store selling roasted coffee and brewing equipment from Bafoussam, and had never backed up his store's data or updated its software beyond the week it first went live, until a plugin update on his own laptop malfunctioned mid-installation and left his product catalogue and two years of order history unreachable for four days. 1.0 Learning Outcomes By the end of this study session, you should be able to: Explain what research found about the cybersecurity threats and defensive practices most relevant to small and medium enterprises. Distinguish a store protected by routine, tested practices from one left exposed by default. Apply a method for backing up, updating and controlling access to a store's data. 2.0 Main Content 2.1 Four Days Without a Catalogue Brice Fotso's coffee business in Bafoussam had never had its store data backed up separately, and its plugins and software had not been updated since the week the store first launched. A routine plugin update, run late one evening, malfunctioned partway through installation and left the entire product catalogue and two years of order history unreachable, with customers unable to browse or even check an existing order's status for four full days while Brice worked to recover it. 2.2 What Research Found About Cybersecurity Threats and Defensive Practices for SMEs Mujtaba Awan and Abu Alam conducted a systematic mapping study reviewing seventy-three articles on cybersecurity threats and defensive strategies facing small and medium firms, published in 2025. Secure backup solutions, access control and automated patch management were identified among the defensive practices most consistently recommended for small and medium enterprises, alongside phishing, ransomware and weak password practices as some of the most prevalent threats they actually face. 2.3 Backing Up, Updating and Controlling Access Keeping a Regular, Tested Backup of the Store's Data Scheduling automatic backups of the store's product catalogue, order history and customer data, stored separately from the store itself, and periodically confirming a backup can actually be restored, turns a single point of failure into a problem that costs hours rather than days. Limiting Who Can Access the Store's Administrative Controls Giving each person who touches the store their own login with only the access their role actually requires, rather than one shared administrator password, makes it possible to see who changed what and to remove access cleanly when someone stops working with the business. 2.4 Key Practices Schedule regular, automatic backups of the store's catalogue, orders and customer data. Store backups separately from the store itself, not on the same system alone. Periodically test that a backup can actually be restored, not just that it was created. Give each person their own login with only the access their role requires. 2.5 A Worked Example: Brice's Backup and Access Routine Once his catalogue was rebuilt, Brice set up an automatic weekly backup stored separately from the store itself, tested it once by deliberately restoring it to a spare account, and replaced the single shared login he had used with his part-time assistant with two separate accounts, each limited to the tasks that person actually handled. Brice had genuinely believed his store was too small to be worth the extra setup a backup routine would take, an assumption that had held for nearly two years before it was tested. The four lost days had nothing to do with the size of his business and everything to do with there being no second copy of its data anywhere else, and only building that second copy afterward ever removed the risk a single failure had exposed. 2.6 Common Pitfalls Treating a store as too small to be worth backing up leaves it exposed to exactly the kind of single point of failure that cost Brice four days of lost access, regardless of how modest the catalogue actually is. Sharing one administrative login among everyone who touches the store makes it impossible to tell who changed what, and leaves no clean way to remove access when someone moves on. 2.7 Protection Is Cheapest Before It Is Needed Brice's coffee had built a loyal following well before the failure, and nothing about the incident changed how customers felt about the product itself. No copy of the store's data had ever existed anywhere but the one place the failure struck, and only building a second copy elsewhere, along with clearer access controls, ever turned a possible repeat of those four lost days into a routine restore. 3.0 Study Session Summary and Conclusion In this study session, you learned to back up, update and control access to a store's data. Study Session 5 turns from protecting the store's data to making the store itself fast, reliable and usable for every visitor who reaches it.

Reflect and Grow — Self-Assessment 1. Think about your own store's data. If it disappeared tomorrow, is there a separate, tested copy anywhere else? 2. Set up a scheduled backup for one real store's data, and test that it can actually be restored. Practical Output: Practical Output A tested backup routine and access-control setup for one real online store. 7.0 References and Further Reading Awan, M., & Alam, A. (2025). Cybersecurity threats and defensive strategies for small and medium firms: A systematic mapping study. Administrative Sciences, 15(12), Article 481. Optional further reading, curriculum-team reviewed: Genesis 41:36, on food being kept in store against the seven years of famine that would come upon the land. Qur'an, Surah Al-Kahf 18:82, on a wall protecting a treasure kept safe for two orphans until they were old enough to claim it.

lessons.title: Study Session 5: Making the Store Fast, Reliable and Accessible to Every Visitor

blocks.text: Introduction Mariem Mint Ahmed has lived with low vision since childhood and sells hand-dyed textiles from Rosso, building and running her own online store entirely by herself, and had built her product pages around photos and a colour-coded size chart with no written descriptions at all, until a customer who also had low vision messaged to say her own screen reader could tell her nothing about the products beyond their price. 1.0 Learning Outcomes By the end of this study session, you should be able to: Explain what research found about accessibility barriers for shoppers with low vision on e-commerce platforms. Distinguish a store that meets minimum accessibility compliance from one that is genuinely usable by a visitor with a disability. Apply a method for writing descriptive alt text and testing a store with assistive technology. Apply a method for improving a store's loading speed and reliability. Recognise the trade-offs between a heavily visual storefront design and genuine accessibility. 2.0 Main Content 2.1 A Screen Reader That Could Only Announce a Price Mariem Mint Ahmed's textile store in Rosso relied entirely on product photos and a colour-coded size chart, with no written alt text on any image and no text label anywhere for a size. A customer who also lived with low vision messaged to explain that her own screen reader, working through the page, could tell her nothing about a single product beyond its listed price, since every other piece of information had been conveyed through an image or a colour alone. 2.2 What Research Found About Accessibility Barriers for Low-Vision Shoppers Bektur Ryskeldiev, Kotaro Hara and Koki Kusano interviewed twelve participants with low vision using a working customer-to-customer marketplace for a 2022 study presented at the ACM SIGACCESS Conference on Computers and Accessibility. Meeting baseline accessibility guidelines was found not to resolve every real barrier low-vision shoppers faced, since problems such as low-contrast or blurry seller-uploaded photos and descriptions missing basic details like colour or size persisted even on platforms that were technically compliant. 2.3 Writing for Assistive Technology and Designing for Speed Writing Alt Text That Actually Describes the Product Writing alt text for every product photo that names the item, its colour and any detail a sighted shopper would notice at a glance, rather than leaving the field blank or filling it with a filename, gives a screen reader something genuinely useful to announce. Testing the Store With a Screen Reader, Not Just by Eye Navigating the store's own product pages and checkout using a screen reader, rather than only checking how the page looks, reveals gaps a visual review alone will never catch. 2.4 Key Practices Write alt text for every product photo that names the item and any detail a sighted shopper would notice. Test the store's own pages and checkout using a screen reader, not only by eye. Avoid conveying information, such as size or availability, through colour alone. Compress images and limit unnecessary page elements to keep loading times short. Check the store's loading speed on an ordinary mobile connection, not only on a fast office connection. 2.5 A Worked Example: Mariem's Rewritten Product Pages Mariem went through every product photo and wrote alt text naming the fabric, the dye pattern and the colour, replaced her colour-coded size chart with one that also labelled each size in text, and asked a friend who used a screen reader daily to walk through the checkout with her listening alongside. Mariem's visual store design had never been built to exclude anyone; it followed the same photo-and-colour approach most sighted shoppers, herself included, would reach for by default. Only a shopper who actually relied on a screen reader could show her exactly where that default fell short, and only rewriting the pages with that same test in mind ever closed the gap between how the store looked and how usable it actually was. 2.6 Common Pitfalls Relying on colour alone to convey information such as size or stock status leaves that information invisible to a shopper who cannot distinguish the colours, exactly the gap in Mariem's original size chart. Treating baseline accessibility guidelines as the finish line, rather than testing with a screen reader directly, can leave real barriers standing even on a technically compliant store. 2.7 Accessible to Everyone Means Tested by Someone Who Needs It Mariem's textiles had always been vivid and carefully made, and no part of the product itself needed to change. The barrier lived entirely in pages built around sight alone, and only testing them with someone who actually used a screen reader ever revealed exactly where a genuinely accessible store needed to be different from one that merely looked complete. 3.0 Study Session Summary and Conclusion In this study session, you learned to make a store fast, reliable and accessible to every visitor, including those using assistive technology. Study Session 6 closes this course by turning to the technical settings that determine whether a store can be found through search at all.

Reflect and Grow — Self-Assessment 1. Think about your own store's product pages. Is any information, such as size or availability, conveyed through colour or image alone? 2. Test one real store's checkout using a screen reader, and rewrite at least three product pages with descriptive alt text. Practical Output: Practical Output A screen-reader test of one real store's product pages and checkout, with at least three pages rewritten to include descriptive alt text. 7.0 References and Further Reading Ryskeldiev, B., Hara, K., & Kusano, K. (2022). Investigating accessibility challenges and opportunities for users with low vision disabilities in customer-to-customer (C2C) marketplaces. Proceedings of the 24th International ACM SIGACCESS Conference on Computers and Accessibility (ASSETS '22), Article 40. Optional further reading, curriculum-team reviewed: Leviticus 19:14, on not cursing the deaf, nor putting a stumbling block before the blind, but fearing God. Qur'an, Surah Abasa 80:1 to 2, on the one who frowned and turned away because the blind man came to him.
Evidence to keep Keep a written note, worksheet, reflection or practical output from this study session. Your progress should show real learning before the quiz.

lessons.title: Study Session 6: Configuring the Store's Technical Visibility Settings

blocks.text: Introduction Karim Trabelsi sells olive oil and hand-thrown pottery from Gafsa through his own online store, and had never touched a single technical setting behind his product pages, no page titles beyond the product name, no image descriptions, no sitemap submitted anywhere, until eight months after launch a search for his own shop's products by name and region returned nothing on the first three pages of results. 1.0 Learning Outcomes By the end of this study session, you should be able to: Explain what research found about the relative importance of technical SEO factors in website ranking. Distinguish a store's content from its technical visibility configuration. Apply a method for configuring a store's technical settings so search engines can find and rank it. 2.0 Main Content 2.1 Eight Months, Three Pages of Search Results, No Sign of the Shop Karim Trabelsi's olive oil and pottery store in Gafsa had launched with every technical setting left at the platform's default, generic page titles built from the product name alone, no written image descriptions, and no sitemap ever submitted to a search engine. Eight months after launch, searching for his own shop's products by name and region, Karim found nothing on the first three pages of results, a gap none of his handful of word-of-mouth customers had ever mentioned to him. 2.2 What Research Found About Technical SEO and Website Ranking Mohammad Khalaf Daoud and six co-authors surveyed 400 respondents for a 2024 study on the strategies that most affect a website's search ranking. Technical SEO, factors such as page loading speed, structured data and a properly submitted sitemap, was found to closely trail keyword relevance in importance for reaching the first page of results, and to matter more than off-page strategies such as backlinks. 2.3 Configuring the Store's Technical Settings Adding Descriptive Page Titles and Image Alt Text Writing a specific page title for every product and category, and descriptive alt text for every image, rather than leaving a platform's default in place, gives a search engine the specific words it needs to match a product to a real search. Submitting a Sitemap and Checking Page Speed Submitting the store's sitemap directly to a search engine, and checking that product pages load quickly, closes two technical gaps a search engine cannot work around no matter how good the product itself is. 2.4 Key Practices Write a specific, descriptive page title for every product and category. Add descriptive alt text to every product image. Submit the store's sitemap to a search engine and check page loading speed regularly. 2.5 A Worked Example: Karim's Technical Configuration Karim rewrote his page titles to name the specific olive oil variety or pottery style on each page, added alt text describing each photo, compressed his largest product images, and submitted his sitemap through a search engine's free tools for the first time since launch. Karim's olive oil and pottery had drawn strong reviews from the handful of customers who found the shop through word of mouth, so nothing about the products themselves needed correcting. A search engine had no technical information anywhere on the site to connect a real search to a real page, and only adding that information directly ever gave the store a chance to appear where a new customer was actually looking. 2.6 Common Pitfalls Leaving a platform's default, generic page titles and blank image descriptions in place gives a search engine nothing specific to match against a real customer's search, precisely the gap behind Karim's invisible shop. Never submitting a sitemap leaves a search engine to discover a store's pages on its own timeline, if it discovers them at all. 2.7 A Store Only Ranks for What It Tells a Search Engine About Itself Karim's products had never been the reason his shop stayed hidden from search results for eight months. The missing piece was technical information a search engine could actually use, page titles, image descriptions, a submitted sitemap, and only adding that information ever gave his store a fair chance of being found by someone searching for exactly what he sold. 3.0 Study Session Summary and Conclusion In this study session, you learned to configure a store's technical settings so it can be found and ranked by search engines. This closes Course 101 and prepares you for Course 102, Store Analytics and Performance Dashboards for Small Enterprises, the next course in Pathway 61.

Reflect and Grow — Self-Assessment 1. Think about your own store. Have you ever searched for your own products the way a new customer would, and checked where your store appears? 2. Rewrite the page title and alt text for at least three real product pages, and submit the store's sitemap if it has not already been done. Practical Output: Practical Output A technical visibility configuration for one real store, including rewritten page titles, alt text and a submitted sitemap. 7.0 References and Further Reading Daoud, M.K., Sharabati, A-A.A., Samarah, T., Alqurashi, D., Alfityani, A., Allahham, M., & Nasereddin, A.Y.
